title: Statue of Liberty Gift
content: The Statue of Liberty was a gift from France to the United States, dedicated in 1886 to commemorate the centennial of American independence.

title: Eiffel Tower Facts
content: The Eiffel Tower was built for the 1889 World's Fair and was initially meant to be a temporary structure. It was almost dismantled in 1909!

title: Statue's Broken Chains
content: At the feet of the Statue of Liberty lie broken chains, symbolizing freedom from oppression and slavery, which are not easily visible from the ground.

title: Great Wall Visibility from Space
content: Contrary to popular belief, the Great Wall of China cannot be seen from the Moon with the naked eye. It can be seen from low Earth orbit under perfect conditions.

title: Great Wall Length
content: The Great Wall of China is approximately 13,171 miles (21,196 kilometers) long, making it the longest wall in the world.

content: As you look up, towering over you is the first of the four Meel-i-Menara — the minarets that stand like vigilant sentinels at the corners of the Taj Mahal. These are not mere decorations, but guardians of this sacred monument, standing watch over the tomb and the legacy it holds. The minarets symbolize protection and strength. Though graceful, they are slightly tilted outward. This intentional design ensures that in the event of an earthquake, they would fall away from the mausoleum, safeguarding the central tomb from harm. Each minaret serves both a functional and symbolic purpose. They echo the tradition of Islamic architecture, where minarets call the faithful to prayer. Here, they elevate the spiritual presence of the Taj Mahal, as though reaching up to the heavens themselves, calling not just for prayer but for remembrance. Imagine this minaret as a steadfast guardian of Shah Jahan’s love for Mumtaz. As he crafted this monument, he knew that love — like this tower — must be protected, preserved from the passage of time. It stands tall, a reminder that even in the most delicate beauty, strength is required to preserve it. Take a moment to admire its symmetry and elegance. This tower is a pillar of love’s endurance, standing strong against the tests of time and fate.

content: As you stand before the Reflecting Pool, known as the Hauz, take a moment to absorb the sight before you. The Taj Mahal, perfectly mirrored in the still water, appears as though it is floating — weightless, timeless, and utterly flawless. Look closely at the reflection. The pool was purposefully designed to capture this image, creating a duality that speaks to the balance between life and death, heaven and earth, reality and illusion. For a brief moment, everything feels aligned — perfectly symmetrical, just as love was in Shah Jahan’s eyes. In Mughal architecture, water symbolizes purity and life. The Hauz here doesn’t just reflect the Taj Mahal; it reflects the soul of the monument and the emotions behind it. It reminds us that true beauty is not only in what is built but in what is mirrored back to us. Pause for a moment. See your own reflection in the water. Just as the Taj’s image is held still in its surface, the love story that built this monument lives on in the hearts of those who come to witness it.
